question: Fix a real point a and a natural number k, and prescribe target values v(0), v(1), ..., v(k). Define a degree-at-most-k real polynomial P by taking the local Taylor polynomial centred at a whose coefficient of (x-a)^j is v(j)/j!. Prove that for every j with 0 <= j <= k the ordinary j-th derivative of P evaluated at a equals exactly v(j). You may use the fact that the j-th derivative of a polynomial at a point equals j! times the degree-j Taylor coefficient of the polynomial about that point.

The key bridge is that for any polynomial Q, (d^j/dx^j Q)(a) = j! * c_j, where c_j is the coefficient of (x-a)^j in the Taylor expansion of Q about a; equivalently c_j is the degree-j coefficient of the shifted polynomial Q(x+a). Step 1: the Taylor coefficients of P about a are read off directly: the coefficient of (x-a)^j is v(j)/j! for j <= k and 0 for j > k, because P is already written in the (x-a) basis. Step 2: apply the bridge at order j <= k: (d^j P/dx^j)(a) = j! * (coefficient of (x-a)^j) = j! * (v(j)/j!). Step 3: since j! is a nonzero natural number cast into the reals, j! * (v(j)/j!) = v(j) exactly. Hence every requested jet value is reproduced, and the construction has degree at most k, has degree at most k. The bound k is the generic (worst-case) degree needed to carry k+1 derivative constraints at a single node; particular data may be realised by a lower-degree polynomial (all-zero data gives the zero polynomial, and if v(k)=0 the degree drops below k), so k is an upper bound on this construction's degree, not a universal minimum for every data vector. No approximation is involved: the identities are exact real-polynomial identities.

question: Two real polynomials p and q both have degree at most 2k+1, and both satisfy the same two-point jet data: all derivatives through order k agree at the node -1, and all derivatives through order k agree at the node 0. The equivalence used is: agreement of all derivatives through order k at a point a is equivalent to (x-a)^{k+1} dividing the difference (one direction is the high-multiplicity-zero fact; the converse is proved by reading Taylor coefficients, all of which through degree k vanish). The same at 0 gives x^{k+1} divides p-q. Step 2 (coprimality combines the two): (x+1)^{k+1} and x^{k+1} are coprime because their bases x+1 and x differ by a unit (their difference is 1), and coprimality is preserved under taking powers. For coprime factors each dividing the same element, their product divides it; hence (x+1)^{k+1} * x^{k+1} divides p-q. Step 3 (degree accounting forces zero difference): the product has degree (k+1)+(k+1) = 2k+2. If p-q were nonzero, a nonzero multiple of a degree-(2k+2) polynomial would have degree at least 2k+2. But deg(p-q) <= max(deg p, deg q) <= 2k+1 < 2k+2, a contradiction. Therefore p-q = 0, i.e. p = q. The degree budget 2k+1 is exactly one below the combined multiplicity 2k+2, which is what makes the only common solution the zero difference; coprimality is what lets the two separate divisibilities multiply.

question: A colleague claims that the two-point jet data 'all derivatives through order k agree at -1 and at 0' pins down a real polynomial uniquely, with no restriction on its degree. Show this is false by exhibiting an explicit nonzero polynomial of degree 2k+2 all of whose derivatives through order k vanish at both -1 and 0. reference_answer: Counterexample: take E(x) = (x+1)^{k+1} * x^{k+1}, a polynomial of degree (k+1)+(k+1) = 2k+2. Step 1: at the node -1, E has the factor (x+1)^{k+1}, i.e. a zero of order k+1 there; hence all derivatives of E through order k vanish at -1 (a zero of order k+1 kills derivatives 0..k). Symmetrically the factor x^{k+1} makes all derivatives through order k vanish at 0. So E carries the all-zero endpoint jet data, exactly the data that the zero polynomial also carries. Step 2: E is not the zero polynomial (it is monic of degree 2k+2), so if p is any solution of a given jet-data problem, p + E is a different polynomial with identical endpoint jets. Thus the solution is not unique once degree 2k+2 is allowed; the colleague's claim fails. Step 3 (exact structure): the solutions of fixed endpoint jet data form a coset of the ideal generated by E = (x+1)^{k+1} x^{k+1}. Within any degree bound 2k+1 the coset meets the degree-<=2k+1 space in exactly one point (that is the uniqueness theorem). Allowing degree 2k+2 adds the one-dimensional direction spanned by E, and more generally allowing degree 2k+1+d adds a d-dimensional family (multiples of E by polynomials of degree < d). So the degree-2k+1 budget is sharp: it is the largest budget on which the jet data has a unique solution.

question: Let the generating series be C(X) = exp(X) * (1 - X)^{-(k+1)} as formal power series over the reals. Prove that its coefficient of X^r is exactly sum_{m=0}^{r} C(k + r - m, k) / m!, where C(.,.) is the binomial coefficient, and prove that this coefficient is nonnegative for every r, with the r=0 coefficient equal to 1. Here [X^m] exp = 1/m! and [X^{i}] (1-X)^{-(k+1)} = C(k+i, k). Step 2 (substitute i = r-m): the convolution becomes sum_{m=0}^{r} (1/m!) * C(k + (r-m), k) = sum_{m=0}^{r} C(k+r-m, k)/m!, which is the asserted closed form. The index substitution is valid because as m ranges over 0..r the complementary index r-m ranges over r..0, covering the same antidiagonal. Step 3 (nonnegativity): every summand is a ratio of a nonnegative binomial coefficient and a positive factorial, hence nonnegative; a finite sum of nonnegative reals is nonnegative. Step 4 (value at r=0): the sum collapses to the single term m=0, giving C(k, k)/0! = 1/1 = 1. This closed form is what makes the truncation A_k the exact finite object underlying the positive source polynomial, and its nonnegativity is exactly the ingredient needed downstream for positivity.

In the first term, (1-t)^{k+1} vanishes to order k+1 at t=1 (the right node), so the entire first term and all its derivatives through order k vanish at p=0; thus the first term is responsible only for the left node. At t=0 the first term equals exp(-1) * 1 * A_k(0); because A_k(0) is the degree-0 coefficient of the generating series, which is 1, the first term contributes exactly exp(-1) at the left node, matching the required left endpoint value exp(-1). question: Let a degree-d polynomial be given by Bernstein coefficients c(0),...,c(d), all lying in a common interval [lo, hi]. Suppose we restrict the polynomial to a subinterval [u, v] with 0 <= u < v <= 1 by two successive de Casteljau subdivisions, producing new Bernstein coefficients c'(0),...,c'(d) for the restricted piece. reference_answer: Two facts drive the proof. Fact A (partition of unity): the Bernstein basis functions of a fixed degree sum to 1 at every t, i.e. sum_{r=0}^{d} B_{d,r}(t) = 1. Fact B (nonnegativity on [0,1]): each B_{d,r}(t) >= 0 for t in [0,1]. Together they say that any Bernstein sum sum_r c(r) B_{d,r}(t) with t in [0,1] is a convex combination of the c(r), hence lies between min and max of the coefficients; in particular if all c(r) in [lo,hi] the value lies in [lo,hi]. Step 1 (one subdivision preserves bounds): each new coefficient produced by a single de Casteljau subdivision at a parameter in [0,1] is itself a Bernstein sum of a sub-row of the original coefficients evaluated at that parameter. By Facts A and B it is a convex combination of coefficients from [lo,hi], hence in [lo,hi]. This applies to the right-edge (upper) subdivision at u in [0,1]: all its outputs stay in [lo,hi]. Step 2 (second subdivision): the left-edge (lower) subdivision is applied at the parameter (v-u)/(1-u). Because 0 <= u < v <= 1 we have 0 <= (v-u)/(1-u) <= 1 (the numerator is nonnegative and at most the positive denominator 1-u). So the second subdivision is again evaluated at a parameter in [0,1], and by the same convex-combination argument its outputs — the restricted coefficients c'(i) — remain in [lo,hi]. Step 3 (conclusion): composing the two bound-preserving subdivisions keeps every c'(i) in [lo,hi]. This is the exact numerical-stability property of de Casteljau subdivision: restricting to a subinterval never amplifies coefficients beyond the original range, in contrast to monomial-basis restriction which can.

question: Let q be a real polynomial and consider sampling it on an arithmetic progression x_j = start + step * j for j = 0,1,...,count-1. Both sums are finite, so Fubini for finite sums lets us exchange them: M = sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r (sum_{j=0}^{count-1} j^r). Step 3 (insert the closed power sum): by the Faulhaber identity sum_{j=0}^{count-1} j^r = P_r(count), a fixed polynomial in count given by Bernoulli numbers. Substituting gives M = sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r P_r(count), a sum of only D+1 = 2 deg(q)+1 terms, independent of count. The only requirement is that the coefficient index runs up to a bound at least D, so that g is fully captured; the identity holds for every count including count = 0 (empty sum = 0 and P_r(0) = 0). question: The target function is strictly positive everywhere and passes through the value 1 at the physical point p = 0 (the splice point). question: Consider a bivariate real array F(x,y) = q(u(x) + v(y)), where q is a real polynomial of degree at most d and u, v are arbitrary real-valued functions of the row index x and column index y respectively. Each summand is a product of a function of x alone, A(x,i) := c_i(u(x)), and a function of y alone, B(i,y) := v(y)^i. Step 3 (read off the matrix product): define A as the (number of rows) by (d+1) matrix with entries A(x,i) and B as the (d+1) by (number of columns) matrix with entries B(i,y). Then (A B)(x,y) = sum_{i=0}^{d} A(x,i) B(i,y) = F(x,y), i.e. F = A * B exactly, with inner dimension d+1. Step 4 (rank bound): the rank of a product A*B is at most the number of columns of A, which is d+1; equivalently the inner dimension bounds the rank. Hence rank F <= d+1. Why the inner dimension is degree-controlled: the only data that produce the finite factorization are the d+1 Taylor coefficients of q; the number of distinct values of u and v (i.e. the matrix dimensions) is irrelevant. The additive structure u(x)+v(y) is essential — it is what lets the single-variable Taylor expansion separate the two indices into a sum of d+1 rank-one pieces. question: A bivariate array is said to 'factor through width w' if it can be written as a product of a (rows x w) and a (w x cols) matrix. One stacks the left factors side by side and the right factors on top of each other (direct sum of inner index sets), so the new inner dimension adds. (ii) Negation: if F factors through w, then -F factors through the same width w; negate one factor (e.g. the left), the inner dimension is unchanged. (iii) Entrywise product: if F factors through w1 and G through w2, their Hadamard product (x,y) -> F(x,y) G(x,y) factors through width w1 * w2; the inner index set is the Cartesian product of the two, with left/right factors multiplied componentwise. Widths multiply. (iv) Scaling: a constant multiple c*F factors through the same width w (absorb c into the left factor). Assembling a width bound: a threshold indicator 1[M u(x) + v(y) < T] factors through width 2 (a two-state prefix/suffix separation across the binary cut); an exponential exp(u(x)+v(y)) factors through width 1 (it splits as a product exp(u(x)) exp(v(y))); a polynomial q(u(x)+v(y)) of degree <= d factors through width d+1 (shifted Taylor). A piece like 'indicator times exponential' uses law (iii): width 2*1 = 2; 'indicator times polynomial' uses (iii): width 2*(d+1). Summing the left-tail, middle, and right-tail pieces uses law (i): the total width is the sum of the pieces' widths. Negation (ii) lets one express a difference of two indicators (a band) and scaling (iv) lets one weight the left tail by exp(-1). Because every law manipulates only the factor matrices and inner index sets, the composite width bound is obtained symbolically, never materialising the full array; the final width is a fixed linear function of the degree d (independent of the array dimensions).

Term 3 (right tail): (1 - 1[n < B]) * exp(-grid), the complement indicator times an exponential; the complement factors through width 2 and the exponential through width 1, so width 2 * 1 = 2. question: A reader argues: 'Since the sampled Hermite amplitude array has every bipartite cut rank bounded by 8k+12, the state can be prepared by a polynomial-resource circuit; the rank bound closes the state-preparation task.' Explain why this inference is not valid as stated. Exhibit the logical gap by distinguishing what a cut-rank/factorization certificate actually provides from what a state-preparation circuit requires, and identify at least two concrete ingredients that the rank bound alone does not supply.
reference_answer: The inference conflates a structural separation certificate with a constructive compilation. What the certificate provides is: for each bipartite cut, an explicit algebraic factorization F = A B with inner dimension at most 8k+12, hence a rank bound. This is a statement about the existence and width of a low-rank decomposition of the sample matrix. What state preparation requires is strictly more: (1) an actual sequence of elementary gates (e.g. uniformly controlled rotations and CX) whose unitary's first column equals the normalized amplitude vector; (2) the real rotation angles — i.e. an isometry/QR-type completion of the low-rank factors into unitary tensors — together with a finite-precision or exact-angle model; (3) handling of normalization by the true global sample norm, which the per-cut factorization does not compute. A low rank per cut is necessary context for an MPS/TT route but not sufficient: a bounded-rank matrix of amplitudes does not come with a canonical-form gauge, an isometrization of the cores, or a bound on the arithmetic/gate cost of realising those cores. Counterexample-style gap: one can have a family of matrices all of rank 1 (the extreme low-rank case) whose entries are arbitrary efficiently-or-inefficiently describable functions; rank 1 alone says nothing about whether the single factor vectors are preparable by a short circuit or even computable to finite precision. Thus 'rank <= 8k+12 for all cuts' is compatible with both easy and hard preparation problems, so it cannot by itself close the task. The source material is explicit that the factorization certificates 'are not a gate compiler, an isometry completion, or a finite-precision algorithm,' and that a rank bound alone does not close the polynomial-resource state-preparation task; the separate normalization supplier and the explicit RY/CX circuit are additional, independent constructions.

question: A gluing principle states: if two real functions f and g are each C^k and all their derivatives through order k agree at a cut point c, then the spliced function (equal to f for x < c and g for x >= c) is C^k. A student claims the jet-matching hypothesis is unnecessary — that merely requiring f and g to be C^k and to agree in value at c (f(c) = g(c)) already gives a C^k splice. Disprove this for k = 1 with an explicit example, and explain exactly which derivative order fails and why the full jet-matching hypothesis through order k is needed for a C^k conclusion.
reference_answer: Counterexample at k = 1, cut c = 0. Take f(x) = 0 and g(x) = x. Both are C^1 (indeed C^infinity), and they agree in value at 0: f(0) = 0 = g(0). The splice is h(x) = 0 for x < 0 and h(x) = x for x >= 0, which is exactly the ReLU function (max(x,0)). Step 1 (continuity holds): h is continuous because the one value-matching condition f(0) = g(0) is satisfied; so h is C^0. Step 2 (first derivative fails): the left derivative of h at 0 is f'(0) = 0, while the right derivative is g'(0) = 1. Since 0 != 1, h is not differentiable at 0, hence not C^1. The student's weakened hypothesis (value agreement only) is therefore insufficient: it controls order 0 but leaves the order-1 jets mismatched. Step 3 (what the real principle needs): to obtain C^1 we must also require f'(0) = g'(0); more generally for C^k we need iterated-derivative agreement at every order j = 0,1,...,k. The proof of the correct principle is by induction on k: the base case uses continuity from value matching; the inductive step differentiates the splice, which is itself a splice of f' and g' (using that the one-sided derivatives coincide precisely because f'(c)=g'(c)), and then applies the hypothesis one order lower. Each induction level consumes exactly one jet-matching equation, so all k+1 equations j = 0,...,k are genuinely used. Dropping any of them breaks the chain at that order, exactly as the ReLU example breaks at order 1. Hence the jet-matching hypothesis through order k is necessary, not decorative, and value agreement alone yields only continuity.

States the correct hypothesis needs derivative agreement at every order j=0..k, not just the value.
Explains the inductive proof consumes one jet-matching equation per order, so each of the k+1 equations is genuinely used.

Hence it fails to be C^1, disproving the weakened claim; C^1 additionally requires f'(c)=g'(c).
The correct C^k gluing is proved by induction consuming one jet-matching equation per order, so all orders 0..k are needed.

question: The target initial datum is the piecewise function equal to exp(p) for p < -1, to the source polynomial S(p) for -1 <= p <= 0, and to exp(-p) for p > 0. Assume it is already known that S matches the required endpoint jets: all derivatives of S through order k equal those of exp at the left junction p = -1, and all derivatives of S through order k equal those of exp(-p) at the right junction p = 0. Prove that the full target is globally C^k for every natural number k, using a reusable two-piece C^k gluing theorem applied twice.
reference_answer: Represent the target as a nested double splice: first glue the polynomial piece to the right exponential at p = 0, then glue the left exponential to that result at p = -1. Step 1 (right junction, p = 0): the polynomial p -> S(p) is C^k (polynomials are C^infinity), and p -> exp(-p) is C^k (composition of exp with negation). The jet-matching hypothesis at p = 0 is given: the derivatives of S through order k equal those of exp(-p) at 0. Here one uses that the j-th derivative of exp(-p) is (-1)^j exp(-p), equal at p=0 to (-1)^j, matching the prescribed right-endpoint jet (-1)^j of S. By the two-piece C^k gluing theorem, the right splice R(p) = (S for p < 0, exp(-p) for p >= 0) is C^k. Step 2 (left junction, p = -1): now glue exp (which is C^k) to R at p = -1. The left exponential exp has j-th derivative exp, equal at p=-1 to exp(-1). On a neighborhood of p = -1 the right splice R coincides with the polynomial S (since -1 < 0, points near -1 are < 0, where R = S), so the derivatives of R at -1 equal those of S at -1, which by hypothesis equal exp(-1) through order k. Thus exp and R satisfy the jet-matching hypothesis at -1. Applying the gluing theorem again, the double splice (exp for p < -1, R otherwise) is C^k. Step 3 (identify with the target): the double splice equals the original piecewise target: for p < -1 it is exp(p); for -1 <= p < 0 it is R = S(p); at p = 0 both the <=0 and >0 conventions give value 1 (S(0) = 1 = exp(0)); for p > 0 it is exp(-p). So the target is exactly the double splice, hence C^k. Since k is arbitrary and the same argument runs for every k, the target is C^k for all k. The construction reuses a single gluing theorem twice, each application discharged by the known endpoint jets; smoothness is thus reduced entirely to the Hermite jet-matching of S.

question: To locate where the left exponential tail meets the polynomial bridge on a grid of 2^n cells, one performs an exact-comparison binary search carrying real interval endpoints: starting from the real interval [lower, lower+span] with span equal to the full width, each of n steps halves the span, forms the midpoint, compares it against the threshold -1, and recurses into the half that still contains the crossing. The search returns an index 'cutIndex'. Prove that this search returns exactly the true cutoff index for every width n and scale L > 0, including the boundary cases where the crossing is at the very first grid point or at the very last, and the single-cell (n = 0) base case. State the exact number of real comparisons and real field operations the search performs.
reference_answer: Model the search by an interval invariant: at a node with 'remaining' halvings left, 'start' already-decided low-order index, and current interval first point gridPoint(start) and width span = step * 2^remaining, assume the true cutoff c = cutIndex satisfies start <= c <= start + 2^remaining (it lies in the current interval). We prove the returned value equals c by induction on 'remaining'. Base case (remaining = 0, one cell): the interval has a single cell starting at 'start'. The search compares the grid point at 'start' against -1. If gridPoint(start) < -1, then 'start' is still below the threshold, so the crossing is at start+1 and the hypotheses force c = start+1; the search returns start+1. Otherwise 'start' is at or past the threshold, so c = start and the search returns start. In both branches the returned value equals c; this also covers the endpoint boundary cases (crossing at the first or last point) because the invariant pins c to one of the two interval ends when the cell is minimal. Inductive step (remaining+1): the search forms the midpoint, which equals gridPoint(start + 2^remaining) (the first point of the upper half), and compares it to -1. If it is below -1, the crossing lies in the upper half, so recurse with start' = start + 2^remaining and the same remaining; the lower bound updates to start' <= c (since the midpoint is still below threshold, c >= start + 2^remaining) and the width halves, preserving the invariant, so by induction the recursion returns c. If it is at or past -1, the crossing lies in the lower half; recurse with the same start and halved width, and the invariant's upper bound tightens to c <= start + 2^remaining, again returning c. The key geometric identities are span/2 = step * 2^remaining and gridPoint(start) + step*2^remaining = gridPoint(start+2^remaining), which make the carried real endpoints exact — no ceiling evaluation or grid enumeration occurs. Starting the top-level search with the full interval [-pi L, 0] and remaining = n satisfies the initial invariant (the cutoff lies between index 0 and the midpoint index 2^n), so the top-level call returns cutIndex exactly. Cost: each of the n internal halvings performs 2 real field operations (one division to halve the span, one addition to form the midpoint) and 1 real comparison; the base level performs 1 comparison. The top-level producer additionally does one multiplication (pi*L) and one subtraction (0 - width) to initialise the interval. Hence the search proper uses exactly 2n field operations and n+1 comparisons; including initialisation the producer uses 2n+2 field operations and n+1 comparisons. Natural-index arithmetic, powers of two, and counter bookkeeping are outside this real-arithmetic cost model; finite-bit comparison of arbitrary real inputs is not claimed.
